name: RadioShack
tierWhy: RadioShack Corporation went into Chapter 11 in 2015 and its successor General Wireless did the same in 2017, but the name is still in use: Unicomer Group has owned the brand since 2023, and it sells online and through dealer and franchise stores.[^15][^26][^30][^31]

title: RadioShack (1921–2015): 5,289 stores to bankruptcy
description: RadioShack ran 5,289 company stores in 2001, lost $400.2M in 2013 and filed for bankruptcy in 2015 and 2017. A Central American retailer now owns the name.

card.blurb: Once a store within a short drive of almost every American. The stores stayed open long after the reason to visit them had moved online.

hero.dates: Founded in Boston in 1921. Filed for Chapter 11 on February 5, 2015. The name is still for sale on shelves.
hero.standfirst: For decades RadioShack was the store within a short drive of almost every American, selling batteries, cables and a part for anything. It kept the stores long after the reason to visit them had moved online and into phone carriers’ hands.
hero.deck: RadioShack was the U.S. [electronics chain](/category/electronics/) that filed for bankruptcy in 2015, with its successor General Wireless following in 2017. At its peak in 2001 it ran 5,289 company stores in the U.S. and about 2,100 more dealer outlets. By 2013 it had lost $400.2M in a year, and its stockholders’ equity had fallen by four-fifths in four years. The brand now belongs to a Central American retailer and lives on through dealer stores and a website. It draws on 20 years of RadioShack’s [10-Ks](#sources), its bankruptcy filings, contemporary press and the archived website.

findings.title: The footprint outlived the business.
findings.text: Company stores peaked at 5,289 in 2001 and were still 4,297 at the end of 2013, while sales per store fell by about a fifth between 2005 and 2013 (derived).[^6][^13]

findings.title: Phones became half the company, on someone else’s terms.
findings.text: Wireless was 28.7% of sales in 2003 and the mobility platform 52.4% in 2013. In 2013 the 10-K blamed falling postpaid phone sales and rising handset costs for a “substantial decrease” in gross profit.[^9][^13]

findings.title: Margins went first.
findings.text: Gross margin was 50.3% in 2004. By our calculation from the 10-K it was 34.1% in 2013.[^8][^13]

findings.title: The cash ran out quickly at the end.
findings.text: Cash fell from $908.2M at the end of 2009 to $43.3M by November 1, 2014. Chapter 11 followed three months later.[^14][^15]

findings.title: The name never died.
findings.text: It has since passed through a hedge-fund affiliate, a second bankruptcy, an e-commerce roll-up that used it for a crypto token, and a Salvadoran retailer that has been a franchisee since 1998.[^26][^28][^30]
